newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies-Oct 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies-Oct 18.

text.p: The National Party has put a security clamp on future coalition discussions after a gaffe by Finance Minister Bill Birch left its caucus concerned the party's inflation policy was up for grabs. Birch came under attack at his party's first post-election caucus meeting after a statement to Reuters Television was interpreted by financial markets as indicating a potential loosening of the 0-2 percent inflation target band. Page 1.

Investors are buying Wilson and Horton shares in an attempt to stop Tony O'Reilly's Independent Newspapers reaching the 90 percent company threshold. Independent analyst Brian Gaynor said purchasers were hoping to extract a better price than the $11 a share offer by relying on Independent Newspapers's need to own 100 percent of Wilson and Horton in order to improve its cashflow. Page 1.

About 538,000 members worldwide of Colonial Mutual Life Assurance Society, including 55,000 from New Zealand, have the chance to vote next month on a proposal to convert the society into a listed public company. The approval is a foregone conclusion, following the offer of free shares and options to members and the recent successful demutualisation and listing of rival National Mutual. Page 8.

The concentration of dairy company ownership under two dominant companies is gathering pace as Cantebury-based South Island Dairy Farmers prepares for merger talks with Hamilton's NZ Dairy Co. Page 8.

AMP Investments, the country's biggest private investor with around $6 billion under management, is to maintain high cash balances in the wake of the uncertain elcection result. However, National Mutual Funds Management is taking a different tack, going "underweight" in cash and "overweight" in shares. Page 9.

Brierley Investments has elbowed its way into the boardroom of Australia's biggest retailer Coles Myer with chief executive Paul Collins making it clear that, unless invited, he would team up with controversial Coles director Solomon Lew and force his way onto the board at the company's November annual meeting. Collins is expected to be nominated as a director after a meeting with Coles directors today. NZ First will begin preliminary talks on Monday, taking the first step in what could be a six week walk towards forming a new government. Talks, on neutral ground, will begin with Labour on Monday. The announcement follows a week of little formal contact between the leaders, but where front-bench MPs from all sides furtively sounding out each other's positions. Both National and Labour are also attempting to work cross-party links through their Maori MPs. More than one third of NZ First's MPs are Maori, making them a powerful force within the caucus.
National's caucus is said to be split between those prepared to go into opposition rather than trade away fundamental principles and those more willing to make deals to retain power. Page 1.

Computer glitches are the culprits for unexpected peaks and troughs in spot electricity prices over the past week, says market operator EMCO chief executive Lincoln Gould. The glitches, now resolved, combined with the inexperience of many of the power companies in using the complex new wholesale electricity market, led to North Island prices soaring this week. Page 7.

Carter Holt Harvey this week broke silence on the long-running court action with its estranged Chilean partner in a $US4.5 billion South American forestry joint venture, saying it was not pursuing the claims simply to ramp up any future bail-out price. Page 9.
